title: Under the broom tree (1 Kings 19:1–8)
hook: exhausted, Elijah wants to die; an angel says eat and sleep
carry: the journey is too great for you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carmel, and a crowd limping between two opinions. Your line was how long, two opinions? Did you take the next step you named? Day seven hundred thirty-three.

One chapter after fire falls from heaven, Elijah is running for his life. Ahab goes home and tells Queen Jezebel everything that happened on Carmel, and she sends Elijah a message: by this time tomorrow, you'll be as dead as the prophets you killed. And the man who stood alone against a crowd simply runs. The text says "he arose, and went for his life." To Beer-sheba, in Judah. He leaves his servant there. Then he walks one more day, alone, into the wilderness, and sits down under a desert bush. Today, under the broom tree.

Under the bush, Elijah asks to die. In the King James Bible: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers." The King James calls the bush a juniper tree; other translations say broom tree. The Bible doesn't hide this moment. A prophet who has just seen fire from heaven is so spent he wants it all to stop. Some readers find that honesty a comfort in itself. Then he lies down and sleeps. And an angel touches him and says only this: "Arise and eat." He looks, and by his head there's "a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water." He eats, he drinks, and he lies down again. The angel lets him. Then comes a second touch, and the line we carry today: "Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee." The angel skips a great deal. No argument. No lecture about Carmel. No correction of his prayer. First sleep, then bread and water, then sleep again, then more bread. And when the angel finally speaks about the road ahead, it's to agree with him: yes, this is too much for you. Not as a rebuke. As a reason to eat. The text goes on: he "went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God." The big conversation, the one about what comes next, waits until he has been fed. One more thing, said plainly: if tiredness ever turns into wanting your life to end, that's the moment to tell someone today, a friend, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live.
screen: `IT IS ENOUGH; TAKE AWAY MY LIFE.`
`THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check on your body before your problems. Settle, and breathe. Ask three plain questions, the angel's kind of questions. When did I last eat something real? When did I last drink water? How did I sleep? Don't judge the answers. Just notice them. Then bring to mind one decision that's been pressing on you, and set it gently to one side, until after a meal and a night's sleep. If you pray, you can rest in the words arise and eat. The bell holds the time.
broom tree. The desert bush where spent and afraid, Elijah asked to die, and an angel answered with bread, water, sleep, and a second touch.
Your line: the journey is too great for you. Today, before you decide anything big, eat a real meal and plan a real night's sleep. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Elijah under the broom tree in times of burnout or depression, and pastors sometimes point to the angel's care, food and sleep before any words, as a model for caring for the exhausted.

original.note: Hebrew: the desert bush Elijah sat under (1 Kings 19:4); the King James says juniper, other translations say broom.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophet having a breakdown.
what it means: after the fire, a spent man asks to die, and an angel answers with bread, water and sleep, twice.
what a scholar hears: the angel's only words are arise and eat, and then the reason: the journey is too great for thee (19:5–7). the talk about what's next waits for Horeb.
